periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem: Read-Aloud and First Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp.67–68): read poem aloud, attend to new words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the title on the board and invites children to guess what the poem might be about, drawing out words like sport, music, and play. Two or three quick responses from the class set a lively tone.
Teacher reads the poem aloud with clear expression and a light rhythm, following the text on Textbook pp.67–68. Children listen with books open and follow along, tracking the words with a finger.
Choral reading round: the class reads the poem together in unison, then in two groups taking alternate stanzas. The teacher models the jaunty pace and children echo it.

Let us Read (pp.67–68): teacher writes the six new words — mistakes, proudly, pace, rhythm, cheerful, swift — on the board. Children read each word aloud, the teacher explains its meaning with a short example sentence, and children repeat.
Quick whole-class recall: teacher asks children to name one child from the poem and what that child does, taking three or four brisk responses to close the encounter on firm ground.

periods.teacher_notes: The alliterative pattern — 'Active Anant', 'Graceful Geeta' — is the poem's most distinctive feature; draw children's attention to the matching first letters of the adjective and the name during the choral read. The new word 'rhythm' may need a physical demonstration: clap or tap the poem's beat while saying the word. Unanchored textbook comprehension questions (task 1, question bank) are not covered in this sitting and may be pointed out to children as reading practice with the poem at home.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Reading Together: Comprehension and Poem Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.69): answer four comprehension questions about the poem.

time_bands.activity: Re-reading for fluency: children read the poem on pp.67–68 aloud once more in pairs, one stanza each, while the teacher listens and assists with pronunciation of 'rhythm' and 'celebrates'.

Let us Think B (p.69): teacher poses the four comprehension questions one by one. For each question children think quietly for a moment, then a volunteer answers while the teacher confirms and elaborates using the poem's exact words. Questions cover Anant's sport, the instruments named, Meena's activity, and Geeta's learning habit.
Pair discussion: teacher asks children to decide with a partner which child in the poem they admire most and why, sharing one reason in a complete sentence. Three or four pairs share aloud.

Closing read-back: teacher re-reads the final three lines — 'Cheerful children everywhere, / playing is a joy! / for every girl and boy' — and asks what message these lines send. Children respond briefly; teacher affirms that the poem includes everyone.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read and chanted the poem together, children are now ready to work with its meaning at the sentence level. Watch for children who confuse Lhamo and Meena — both are connected to music; the distinction is that Lhamo plays a guitar/sitar while Meena sings in rhythm. Encourage children to point to the relevant stanza in the textbook before answering, building the habit of returning to the text.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Talk About Yourself: Sport, Music, and Dance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think C (p.69): discuss games, instruments, and dance forms children know.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the poem's five children and their activities using the textbook, then tells the class: 'Now we will talk about ourselves — the games we play, the music we like, the dances we know.' Children are invited to think silently for a moment.

Let us Think C (p.69), questions 1 and 2: teacher asks 'Which game do you generally play in school?' and 'Do you enjoy indoor or outdoor games more?' Children respond in turn; the teacher models a full-sentence answer first ('I generally play…') and children use that frame.

Let us Think C (p.69), questions 3 and 4: guided conversation about musical instruments — which ones children like or have seen. Teacher lists instruments named on the board as children speak, keeping the energy brisk.

Let us Think C (p.69), question 5: children share their favourite dance form and name a dance from their region or district. Teacher celebrates diversity of answers and connects back to the poem's inclusive closing lines.

periods.teacher_notes: The oracy tasks are anchored in children's own experience, so every child has something genuine to say — the goal is fluency and confidence in complete sentences, not correctness of content. If a child struggles to name a regional dance, accept the district's language name and help the class repeat it; this models that all cultural knowledge is valid. Keep the pace conversational so that shy children are drawn in by the lively atmosphere rather than put on the spot.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard (for listing instruments and dances)

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Adjectives in Action: Match, Observe, and Name

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.69): observe alliterative quality descriptors and write one for your own name.
Let us Learn A (p.70): match adjectives to nouns; learn the term 'adjective'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'Active Anant' and 'Graceful Geeta' on the board and asks: 'What kind of word is Active? What does it tell us?' Children discuss briefly; teacher introduces the word 'adjective' as a describing word and points to its examples in the poem.

Let us Think A (p.69): teacher models the pattern aloud — 'I am Thankful Teacher Tara' — then invites each child to think of one quality adjective that starts with the same letter as their own name and write it in their notebook. Several children share with the class.

Let us Learn A (p.70): teacher reads the five adjective–noun pairs from the textbook and asks children to think before matching. Class works through the matching activity together, with volunteers explaining why each pair belongs together — for instance, 'A sky is blue, so blue goes with sky.'
Quick recall game: teacher calls out a noun from the poem or the match activity and children call back an adjective for it. The exercise closes the adjective concept on a playful note.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the poem's five children and their qualities, children already have an intuitive sense of describing words — this sitting makes that intuition explicit. The alliterative quality task is deliberately personal, so accept any reasonable adjective even if the child needs help with spelling; the target here is understanding the concept, not perfect orthography. For the matching activity, watch for children who match by meaning alone without checking the noun — prompt them to read the noun aloud first.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write D (p.72): find rhyming words for five words from the poem.
Let us Write D (p.72): match five words to their meanings using words from the box.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn B (p.70): fill in blanks with nouns for given adjectives and adjectives for given nouns — complete all eight blanks in the notebook.

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: teacher reads a stanza from the poem and pauses before the rhyming word — 'even when the ground is… ?' Children call out the rhyme. Two or three rounds establish the idea of rhyming pairs firmly before written work begins.

Let us Write D (p.72), rhyming words: children open the textbook and locate the five words — hockey, skates, guitar, race, joy. They find the rhyming partner for each in the poem and write the pairs in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and prompts children who lose their place in the poem.

Let us Write D (p.72), word meanings: teacher reads each meaning sentence aloud and gives children a moment to choose from the box (Brave, Rocky, Mistakes, Proudly, Delightful). Class compares answers and teacher confirms, drawing attention to how context clues in the meaning sentence point to the correct word.

Pair check: children swap notebooks with a partner and verify each other's rhyme and meaning answers using the poem and the textbook. Any disagreements are resolved by re-reading the relevant stanza together.

periods.teacher_notes: The rhyming-word task is grounded in the poem children have already read and chanted, so the answers are locatable by re-reading rather than by guessing — encourage children to scan the poem rather than recall from memory. The word-meanings task introduces the words 'proudly' and 'delightful', which are not everyday words for this age group; give a brief contextual sentence for each ('Shabana felt proudly after winning the race') to anchor meaning before children match. The Let us Learn B fill-in task is set as independent reinforcement at home since the class time is fully used by the two in-class tasks.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Double-Letter Words: Picture Prompt and Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p.71): look at the parrot picture and fill in blanks with double-letter words.
Let us Write B (p.71): think of five kitchen items with double letters and write them.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'village' on the board, underlines the double-l, and says: 'Some words have two of the same letter side by side — these are called double-letter words.' Children brainstorm two or three more examples aloud — bell, egg, room — as a quick warm-up.

Let us Write A (p.71): children look at the parrot illustration on p.71. Teacher reads the sentence frame aloud — 'This is my pet ___. It loves to eat ___, which are ___ in colour.' — and children think about which double-letter words fit each blank. Class shares answers and writes them in their notebooks, teacher confirming and explaining.

Let us Write B (p.71): children close their eyes briefly and picture their kitchen at home, then list five things they know or can think of that have double letters — examples: butter, egg, coffee, bottle, apple. Each child writes five items in their notebook independently, then shares one with the class.

Gallery read-aloud: teacher invites five volunteers to read one of their kitchen double-letter words. The class listens, the teacher writes the words on the board, and together they identify and circle the double letters. Children add any new words they like to their own list.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often know double-letter words from everyday vocabulary without having noticed the spelling pattern — the goal of this sitting is to make that pattern visible and intentional. For Let us Write A, accept parrot (the illustration), seeds, green as likely answers, but also validate other plausible double-letter words that fit the sentence logically. If children struggle with Let us Write B, allow them to call out words they know from any context, not only the kitchen, and then help the class verify whether each truly has a double letter.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Exploring and Doing: Cooking Without Fire and the Paralympic Games

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.71): organise a 'Preparing a Dish Without Fire' activity in class.
Let us Explore (p.72): find out about the Paralympic Games and share points with the class.

time_bands.activity: Let us Explore (p.72): teacher introduces the Paralympic Games with two or three spoken facts — 'These are international sports competitions for athletes with physical disabilities; they are held every four years alongside the Olympics.' Children are asked to recall any athlete or sport they may have heard of and share briefly.

Children work in pairs to discuss two things they would like to find out about the Paralympic Games — e.g. which sports are included, which country hosts them, whether India participates. Each pair shares one question and one fact they already know; teacher writes key facts on the board to build a shared reference.

Let us Do (p.71): the class organises a 'Preparing a Dish Without Fire' activity. The teacher guides groups to prepare a simple no-cook dish — such as a fruit chaat or a biscuit-and-spread snack — using ingredients brought to class. Groups plan their dish briefly, prepare it, and present it to the class with a one-sentence description.

Closing circle: each child uses one sentence to connect the two activities — sport and food — to the poem's theme of a fit, joyful life. The teacher draws the sitting to a close by revisiting the poem's final lines: 'playing is a joy! / for every girl and boy.'

periods.teacher_notes: The 'Preparing a Dish Without Fire' activity works best when ingredients are simple and ready to use — sliced fruit, biscuits, yoghurt, or roasted items — so that children focus on the creative and social experience rather than logistics. For the Paralympic Games discussion, children need not have researched in advance; the pair-talk draws on whatever they already know and the teacher's introductory facts, making the activity self-contained. Both tasks connect organically to the poem's celebration of every child's capacity for joyful, healthy activity.
materials: Simple no-cook food ingredients (fruit, biscuits, or similar)

items.source_section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
items.source_lo: Student locates and retrieves specific information using a celebratory poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five named children — Anant, Geeta, Lhamo, Shabana, Meena — their sports, instruments, and rhythm.
items.item_stem: In the poem, Shabana wins a race. What kind of race does she win, and how does she feel afterwards?

options.label: A
options.text: She wins a cycle race and happily celebrates her fastest pace.

options.label: B
options.text: She wins a hockey match and joins Anant on the field.

options.label: C
options.text: She wins a running race and proudly thanks her coach.

options.label: D
options.text: She wins a swimming race and feels tired.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Child may be confusing Shabana's race with a different sport or character.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child has the sport wrong; may be blending Shabana's stanza with the poem's general theme.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has confused Shabana with Anant, who plays hockey.

items.source_section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
items.source_lo: Student locates and retrieves specific information using a celebratory poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five named children — Anant, Geeta, Lhamo, Shabana, Meena — their sports, instruments, and rhythm.
items.item_stem: Lhamo and his friend both play musical instruments in the poem. Name the two instruments and explain what Lhamo is doing while his friend plays.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Lhamo proudly plays a guitar, while his friend joins him with a sitar. Lhamo plays the guitar as the two friends make music together.

items.source_section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
items.source_lo: Student expresses personal experience and opinion using a guided-conversation frame as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Games, indoor vs outdoor preference, musical instruments, regional dance forms.
items.item_stem: Listen to your teacher's question and choose the answer that best matches what you would say: 'Do you prefer playing an indoor game or an outdoor game?'

options.text: A child can only enjoy one kind of game, never both.
An indoor game is one that is played inside, such as chess or carrom.
Outdoor games are played inside a building with a roof.
You can play cricket indoors without any change to the rules.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 2 is true: an indoor game is played inside, such as chess or carrom. Statements 1, 3, and 4 are false — outdoor games are played outside, cricket cannot be played indoors normally, and children may enjoy both kinds of games.

items.item_stem: Tell the class: name one game you enjoy playing at school, say whether it is indoor or outdoor, and share one reason you enjoy it. Speak in two or three complete sentences.

expected_elements: Names a specific game they play at school.
Correctly identifies it as indoor or outdoor.
Gives a genuine personal reason for enjoying it.

items.item_stem: Read the sentences below. Fill in each blank with a word that has double letters.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Blank | Sentence | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The children played with a red ___ in the park. | ___ |
| 2 | Meena put fresh ___ on her bread for breakfast. | ___ |
| 3 | The puppy wagged its ___ happily. | ___ |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — ball; 2 — butter (or similar accepted double-letter food word); 3 — tail is not a double-letter word, so accept: puppy wagged its fluffy / little — teacher should accept any double-letter word that fits naturally. Correct double-letter words: ball, butter, puppy itself if re-read, egg, bottle, etc.

items.item_stem: Think about the Paralympic Games and the poem's idea that sport and play belong to everyone.
